newsitem.title: USA: Gold drops to 12-year low, oil and cocoa fall.
newsitem.headline: Gold drops to 12-year low, oil and cocoa fall.

text.p: Gold prices slumped to a 12-year low on Thursday after news that the Australian central bank had sold 167 metric tons of gold reserves in recent months.

In other markets, oil prices fell as Iraq moved a step closer to resuming sales under a deal with the United Nations, cocoa prices fell as speculators cashed in profits, and wheat prices fell on reports on excellent yields in Kansas.
At the COMEX in New York, gold for August delivery closed down $7.10 an ounce at $325.20 after setting a new life-of-contract low at $324.00.

"The Australian disposal was a forward sale arranged some time ago with only the deliveries occurring now, so you could argue the market has already at least partly discounted it," said Refco New York economist James Steel.
"But it confirms that central banks worldwide, not just European central banks, are mobilizing their gold reserves to achieve better returns," Steel said.
A strong dollar and rising U.S. stock market, along with low inflation, have turned investors away from gold since gold hit a seven-year peak of $417.00 in February 1996.

Periodic sales of gold by European central banks since last year have hung over the market, with Belgium confirming a 203-ton sale in March 1996 and Holland a 300-ton sale in January 1997. Then came Thursday's news of a 167-ton sale, equivalent to 5.36 million troy ounces, by the Reserve Bank of Australia.
Australia produces about 300 tons of gold a year, making it the world's third-largest gold producer.

"A country in Australia's position, with large gold reserves in the ground and high annual production, derives negligible benefits from holding a significant proportion of its international reserves in the form of gold," the Reserve Bank said in a statement confirming the sales.
It said 125 tons had been delivered in June with the balance to be delivered in August and September this year, spurring speculators to sell futures in a flurry.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices ended sharply lower on news that Iraq had moved a step closer to resuming oil sales under its deal with the United Nations.

Crude oil for August delivery closed 78 cents lower at $19.56 a barrel. Refined products tracked crude, with August gasoline closing down 1.37 cents at a gallon at 57.92 cents and August heating oil down 2.16 cents at 52.76 a gallon.

On Thursday, Iraq's U.N. coordinator Staffan de Mistura said the food distribution plan for Iraq's oil-for-food deal with the U.N. had finally been completed. He indicated it would be submitted for final approval to the U.N soon.

In May, Iraq was permitted by the U.N. to resume oil sales on June 8 under a plan by which Iraq can sell up to $2 billion worth of oil every six months to buy food, medicine and other humanitarian aid. Iraq earned about $1.3 billion in the first six months of the deal which ended on June 7.

"The market had gotten overdone and was due for a correction, and that Iraq story had gotten the ball rolling," said Tom Bentz, energy analyst with High Yield Analytics in New York. "Traders don't want to get too long in case the plan is submitted to the U.N. over the weekend."

At New York's Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, cocoa prices fell sharply for a third consecutive day as speculators cashed in positions ahead of the long U.S. holiday weekend on sentiment that a month-long rally had ended.
September cocoa closed $52 lower at $1,562 per metric ton. The contract has dropped nine percent over the last three days.
A growing consensus that next season's West African harvest would fare better than originally thought set the stage for the downturn, analysts said.
"I think the market basically came to its senses in the last couple of days," said Steve Platt, senior analyst with Dean Witter in Chicago.
"The market recognizes that the (1997/98) Ivory Coast crop is not experiencing any problems and could well come out where it was this year," Platt said.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat prices fell on excellent harvest progress for winter wheat and reports of excellent wheat yields, especially in the key U.S. hard red winter wheat state of Kansas.
September wheat closed at $3.27-1/2, down 5 cents a bushel, after setting a life-of-contract low at $3.27.

"Some wheat numbers of 425 to 450 million bushels (in Kansas) are being talked about, versus 45 days ago where 100 million less at about 325 to 350 million were discussed," said Dave Armstrong, analyst for ABN Amro-The Chicago Corp.
The Kansas hard red winter wheat crop was hit by a freeze in mid-April but nearly perfect weather since then allowed the crop to recover.
